fields.why_it_matters: Dovipie Inn is the most-visible non-homestay establishment inside Khonoma — a guesthouse with two distinct dining rooms.
fields.insider_tip: Reserve Nusi Ba lunch a day ahead.

fields.why_it_matters: When Khonoma was declared Asias First Green Village in 2005 the Angami village council banned commercial hunting and logging and replaced the income with a community-run homestay network.
fields.insider_tip: Booked via the Khonoma Tourism Board.

fields.why_it_matters: The only stand-alone cafe in Khonoma listed on Tripadvisor — Khonoma's dining infrastructure is otherwise homestay kitchens. Located in the Merhuma Khel (one of the village's three khels). Tripadvisor's 'Travelers' Choice' marker sits on it though review count is low; The Better India and Nexplore Travel both cite UKU specifically as the village's cafe stop for noodles and tea.
fields.insider_tip: Hours are unpredictable — call ahead through your homestay host or the village tourism committee. Best for a tea-and-noodles break between the heritage walk and the rice terraces; full meals are still better at your homestay.

fields.signature_dish: Angami-style smoked pork with bamboo shoot
fields.why_it_matters: Khonoma's only proper inn (the Tourist Lodge equivalent) — most-cited dining stop in the village beyond homestays. Tripadvisor 4.4/5 across 163 reviews. Dovipie's kitchen serves Angami-Naga homestyle dishes — pork curry with fermented bamboo shoots, fish chutney, wild apple juice, homemade aubergine pickle. Reviews flag the menu as 'limited' — that's the whole point: 4-5 honest dishes, not a multi-cuisine card.
fields.insider_tip: Order meals at check-in or one hour ahead — kitchen is single-cook, no walk-in service. Rooms ~₹800/night with shared bathrooms; ask Apenyu (the host family) for the wild-apple drink in season (Sep-Nov).

fields.why_it_matters: Run by Vikepeno and Apeno Pier — Apeno is the cook, recurring across Tripadvisor and Homestays of India reviews as the headline reason guests rebook. Vegetables come from the family's terrace fields, rice from their own paddy. Naga thali, smoked pork, axone-cooked greens — village-kitchen scale, but the most consistent food story in any Khonoma homestay write-up.
fields.insider_tip: Walk-ins occasionally accepted for lunch if you call ahead through the homestay number — the Piers also host longer stays. Apeno is a willing teacher; ask her to walk you through the axone fermentation jars, then order whatever's been simmering longest.

fields.why_it_matters: One of the oldest tribal-cuisine kitchens in Kohima, serving Lotha dishes since 1994 from a tiny old-NST-market spot opposite Domino's. Cited by MorungExpress as the address for 'wonderful Lotha dishes' — bamboo shoot pork, smoked beef, anishi — at thali prices, before pan-Naga restaurants made the cuisine touristy.
fields.insider_tip: Open Mon-Sat 10am-7pm only — closed Sundays, and the kitchen runs out by mid-afternoon. Ask for whatever's been smoked that week; if anishi (yam-leaf cake) is on, order it — most pan-Naga places skip it.

fields.why_it_matters: Nagaland's first homegrown coffee-roasting company, founded 2016 by Lichan Humtsoe and his wife. Sources beans exclusively from four Nagaland districts — Kohima, Mokokchung, Mon and Wokha — and runs a stated 'Justice in a cup' ethics chain (no exploited growers, sustainable employment). The Billy Graham Road bar is the roastery flagship.
fields.insider_tip: Ask which Nagaland district the day's pour-over is from — the Mon and Wokha lots taste very different from the Kohima beans. Billy Graham Road itself is a piece of trivia: built in 1972 for the only crusade Billy Graham held in Northeast India, this is the only road in the world named after him.

fields.why_it_matters: Government-run hotel restaurant on P.R. Hill, operating since 1988 under the Nagaland tourism department. Multi-cuisine kitchen (Indian, Chinese, Naga) — useful as a one-stop dining option for traveling families that want a Naga thali alongside familiar Indian food. Long-stayer on every Kohima foodie roundup.
fields.insider_tip: Naga thali is the headline order — at government rates, this is the cheapest sit-down Naga thali in town. The hotel itself is dated, but the kitchen is dependable. Wide vegetarian options.

fields.why_it_matters: The most-cited Naga ethnic-food address near the ISBT bypass — a wood-and-bamboo-and-stone structure built to feel like a traditional morung. Menu pairs smoked-pork momo and kokhü (sticky rice cake) with a coffee bar; an attached lounge runs live bands on selected evenings. Ranked #5 of 33 Kohima restaurants on Tripadvisor (4.8/5).
fields.insider_tip: It's on the bypass, not in the main bazaar — 10 minutes by cab from MG Marg, and easier to access if you're driving in from Dimapur. Order the smoked-pork momo + kokhü combo; the coffee is genuinely the best in this part of town.

fields.why_it_matters: Owner Pelevotuo Solo grew up in his mother's galho restaurant and opened Mom and I Cafe in tribute — 'Mom' is the senior galho cook, 'I' is the cafe's modern Asian-Naga menu. Galho (a one-pot Naga rice porridge with smoked meat and herbs) is the headline dish; the kitchen also runs Taiwanese beef noodles for the millennial crowd.
fields.insider_tip: Order the galho if you've never had it — it's the dish most tourist menus skip. The peppery fried rice is the locals' default lunch order. First-floor space, look for the United Traders building near KAK Store.

fields.why_it_matters: Cited by Tripadvisor reviewers as 'an oasis of North Indian food in Kohima' and 'the first and only place where you can get the naan and tandoori item' — a useful reset for travellers four days into Naga smoked-pork rotation. Ranked #4 of 33 Kohima restaurants. Kitchen claimed and managed by the owner.
fields.insider_tip: Menu is on paper (per Tripadvisor) — staff bring it to the table, no QR codes. The tandoori section is what to order; their dal-and-naan plate fixes any mountain-stomach situation.

fields.why_it_matters: One of Kohima's best-rated mid-range restaurants — Tripadvisor 4.5/5, ranked among Nagaland's top 10. Fuses traditional Naga (axone pork, Naga raja mirchi chutney) with Chinese and contemporary plates; ambiance reads casual-sophisticated rather than rustic. The kitchen cooks to order rather than holding pre-cooked food.
fields.insider_tip: Reviews flag long ticket times (often an hour) and items going off the menu at busy hours — go before 7.30pm or after 9pm to avoid the wait. Order the axone pork curry; locals consider it the litmus-test dish for any Kohima multi-cuisine kitchen.

fields.why_it_matters: Kohima's most-visible pan-Asian outlet — sushi, dim sum, ramen-adjacent noodle bowls in a city where Asian usually means Chinese-Naga fusion. Open 11am-8pm daily. Justdial-rated 3.8/5 across 36 reviews; mixed signal on consistency, strong on the ambition.
fields.insider_tip: Stick to the dim sum and noodle dishes; the sushi is hit-or-miss in a hill town with no daily fish supply. Closes at 8pm — earlier than most Jail Colony spots, so plan dinner before 7pm.

fields.why_it_matters: Billed as 'Kohima's first cocktail dining restaurant' and ranked #2 of 33 Kohima restaurants on Tripadvisor (5.0/5, 9 reviews). Italian-international plates plus modern Naga tasting bites and a proper cocktail list — the city's go-to for date-night and out-of-town business dinners.
fields.insider_tip: Reservations recommended on weekend evenings — the dining room fills fast. Order the pizza (reviewers consistently flag it) and at least one cocktail; the bar is what sets it apart from Kohima's other Italian attempts.

fields.why_it_matters: Ranked #1 of 34 Kohima restaurants on Tripadvisor for several years running. Owner-roaster Dili Khekho keeps the menu deliberately tight — organic, fresh-roasted coffee beans, fresh-baked pastries, waffles. Wood-touch interiors, small terrace overlooking the Jail Colony road; dependable Wi-Fi makes it the de facto remote-work spot in Kohima.
fields.insider_tip: Coffee comes out at café-grade — order an espresso or filter, not the milk-heavy options. Get there before 11am for the freshest pastry batch; the terrace fills up by mid-afternoon.

fields.why_it_matters: P.R. Hill cafe with a strong Korean-Asian lean — Korean kimbap and noodles alongside stir-fried beef, pork ribs and sliders. Founders profiled by Roots and Leisure for putting their own spin on pan-Asian rather than copying Chinese-Naga staples. Cosy room, clear 'Kohima feels' design.
fields.insider_tip: The kimbap and Korean noodles are what set it apart — most other Kohima cafes don't run those. Belho Complex on P.R. Hill — a 5-minute uphill walk from the Hotel Japfu side.

fields.why_it_matters: Elevated cafe near the Commonwealth War Cemetery (one of Kohima's two WWII anchor sites — the Battle of Kohima cemetery). Window seats deliver what reviewers call a 'breathtaking glimpse of Kohima town.' Mixed Naga + continental menu; popular with the youth crowd for momos and pizza.
fields.insider_tip: Service is famously slow — go for the view, not the speed. Pair it with a 30-minute walk through the Commonwealth War Cemetery just below: the WWII Battle of Kohima 'tennis-court' line is at the cemetery's centre.

fields.why_it_matters: Long-running budget cafe at Main Market Junction — cited by MorungExpress as a Kohima foodie staple. Multi-cuisine (Chinese, continental, Naga) with momo as the headline. 509 online reviews, 3.9/5 — far cheaper than the Jail Colony spots, ₹200-400 for two.
fields.insider_tip: Hours are tight — 11am to 5pm only, so this is a daytime stop, not dinner. Order the momos and the filter coffee; the burgers and pizza get inconsistent reviews.

fields.why_it_matters: Casual cafe with a strong American/Chinese menu — Tripadvisor 4.2/5 (#7 of 18 Kohima restaurants on the older list), and a popular hangout for Kohima's college crowd. The newer 'Fifa Restaurant 2.0' offshoot runs the same kitchen template at higher capacity.
fields.insider_tip: Bring a group — it's a hangout-style room, not a date spot. Order the fried chicken and milkshakes; that's what the regulars come for, not the pasta.

fields.why_it_matters: Razhu Point cafe with a pizza-and-momo menu and a few useful vegetarian options (sandwiches, soups) for travellers who want a break from smoked pork. Mid-tier on Tripadvisor (3.1/5, ranked #16 of 18), better-rated locally — Razhu Point itself is one of Kohima's main residential pockets.
fields.insider_tip: Stick to the pizza and pork momo — the wider menu gets inconsistent reviews. Razhu Point is a useful stop if you're staying in that part of town and don't want to taxi to Jail Colony.

fields.why_it_matters: All-day dining inside Niraamaya Retreats Aradura — Kohima's only luxury wellness resort, built into the Aradura ridge. The Café Samsara kitchen runs authentic Naga (smoked pork-bamboo, axone) alongside continental and Asian; halal-certified for Chinese, Nepalese and European cuisines. The most consistent fine-dining option in Kohima for non-residents who book in advance.
fields.insider_tip: Non-residents can dine here but call ahead — the kitchen runs on resort cadence. Order the smoked pork with bamboo shoot (the property's signature) plus one continental plate; the European section is genuinely competent, unlike most Kohima 'continental' menus.

fields.why_it_matters: Hotel restaurant inside De Oriental Grand on High School Road — one of the central Kohima hotels with a sit-down dining room serving Naga ethnic cuisine alongside Indian and Chinese. 30 guest rooms above; the kitchen runs all day for hotel residents and walk-ins.
fields.insider_tip: Useful if you're staying anywhere on High School Road or near Themezie — saves the walk to Jail Colony. Ask the staff which Naga dishes are running fresh that day; the menu rotates with the kitchen's smoking schedule.

fields.why_it_matters: Owner Eden Kichu has run The Restaurant on I.M. Road for over two decades — the longest-running family-run eatery in Mokokchung's Sangtemla Ward. Started as a humble family kitchen, now the town's default 'crowded at lunchtime' meet-up. Menu spans Ao-Naga ethnic cooking, Chinese and South Indian; the special mixed fried rice and mushroom soup are the regulars' default order.
fields.insider_tip: Open 9am-5.30pm — strictly a daytime/lunch room, not for dinner. Eden's the host and remembers names; mention you've come from Kohima and ask which Ao dishes are running fresh. Don't skip the cupcakes from the confectionery side.

fields.why_it_matters: Owned by Temsuienla, a young Mokokchung entrepreneur who built Bambusa around clean atmosphere, fresh ingredients and an 'Asian with a local Naga twist' menu. Thukpa, momo and chowmein are the headline dishes; she's added a Bambusa Express offshoot for faster service.
fields.insider_tip: 9am-8pm daily. The Arkong Ward location puts it in walking distance of most Mokokchung budget hotels. Order the thukpa over the chowmein — the broth has a Naga-pepper edge that the noodles don't.

fields.why_it_matters: Mokokchung's top-rated dinner spot — 5/5 on Restaurant Guru across 76 reviews — and the only kitchen in town running Machihan (Lotha chilli curry) on the menu most nights. Fusion approach: Naga ethnic dishes, Chinese, Italian. Rooftop dining room atop Kichuzar Complex; family-friendly with a cozy Mokokchung-night feel.
fields.insider_tip: Open Mon-Sun 10am-8pm — book ahead for buffet nights. Order Machihan if it's on; outside Wokha, this is one of the few places it appears on a printed menu. The Ayatai mocktail uses local berries, worth a try.

fields.signature_dish: Top Floor Special fried rice with beef chilli
fields.why_it_matters: Run by couple Alemkaba Jamir and Kirensungla Pongen — opened as a 'shared dream' venture and rebuilt after a kitchen fire. Kiren is the cook; her Top Floor Special fried rice (with beef chilli) and Alem's garlic fried rice with hot wings are the menu signatures. Cosy, warm decor; popular with younger Mokokchung crowd.
fields.insider_tip: Open 10.30am-8pm. Casual hangout, not a date room — go for lunch with the friend you're traveling with. The fried rice variants are what to order; skip the longer chowmein menu.

fields.why_it_matters: Slurrp-cited as Mokokchung's headline cafe — 'passion immersed in good books and music.' Menu mixes Asian sushi-momo plates with Mimi singju (a Manipuri-style spicy salad rare in Nagaland menus) and a strong cake/dessert section. Most cited cafe in Mokokchung roundups; the only spot in town consistently described as 'comfortable ambience.'
fields.insider_tip: 9am-8pm daily. Beams Fiery Momos and Mimi Singju are the two non-default orders worth coming for — the chowmein-fried-rice spine of the menu is solid but available everywhere.

fields.why_it_matters: Hilltop hotel restaurant with views over Mokokchung — the only sit-down dining room in town with a separate 'morung'-style seating area in the car park, an in-house veranda over reception and a fish-pond courtyard. Multi-cuisine: Naga, Indian, Chinese. Open all day for hotel guests and walk-ins.
fields.insider_tip: Meals must be ordered at least one hour in advance — call before you walk over. Portions are generous, prices a touch higher than town-centre kitchens. Ask for the Naga thali and a window/morung seat for the hill view.

fields.why_it_matters: The Konyaks Kitchen is the most reliably-open sit-down restaurant in Mon Sadar — run by a Konyak family using their grandmothers Naga chili chutney recipe.
fields.insider_tip: Do not skip the naga chili chutney.

fields.why_it_matters: Mon district has almost no commercial restaurants — Helsa Cottage's kitchen is the most-cited dining option in town. Property is run by the head-woman of the family; 'Helsa' is an acronym of her five children's names (Hamwang, Ethiel, Lemnon, Suzanne, Angam). Konyak cottages with a shared kitchen serving traditional slow-cooked pork and bamboo-shoot dishes; Outlook Traveller, Tripadvisor and multiple tour operators flag it as the de facto food stop for Mon-Longwa travellers.
fields.insider_tip: Order meals at check-in or by phone the day before — the kitchen runs a fixed menu, not à la carte. Veg can be arranged but the pork is what they're known for. Tariffs ~₹1000-1500 a night with meals charged separately.

fields.why_it_matters: Hilltop resort restaurant with panoramic views over Mon town — modern cottage-resort built around Konyak architectural cues. Kitchen runs local Konyak delicacies plus continental options for travellers who can't do back-to-back smoked pork. Complimentary breakfast included for guests; non-guests can dine on call-ahead.
fields.insider_tip: Useful as a sit-down option if you're not staying at Helsa Cottage — call ahead, mention you're a non-resident, and ask whether the day's smoked pork has been done with axone or bamboo shoot. They also run a budget dormitory above if Helsa is full.

fields.why_it_matters: Tea-estate retreat (est. 1988) outside Shiyong village in Sayeang Tea Estate, run by Phejin Konyak — great-granddaughter of the tattooed headhunter Ahon (one of the first interpreters in J.H. Hutton's 1923 Naga Hills tours) and author of 'The Konyaks: Last of the Tattooed Headhunters' (Roli Books, Silver Award London Book Fair 2018). Phejin cooks for guests herself, sharing stories from her fieldwork during meals.
fields.insider_tip: Booking-only — meals are part of the stay package, not walk-in. Drive ~30km from Mon town; pair with a Longwa visit on the same trip. Phejin's book is on the shelf; ask her to walk you through the tattoo glossary at dinner.

fields.why_it_matters: Inside Longwa — the famous Konyak village whose chief's (Angh's) house spans the India-Myanmar border. Jeilei's homestay has a massive kitchen with a central fireplace where food is slow-cooked Konyak-style. Outlook Traveller and FootLooseDev cite it as the cleanest, friendliest kitchen in Longwa for backpackers and tribal-travel groups.
fields.insider_tip: Roughly ₹600/bed and ₹180-200 per meal (veg/non-veg). Sit at the central fireplace, sip the black tea slowly, and let the food come when it comes — the kitchen runs on family rhythm, not service speed. Longwa has no hotels; this is the food infrastructure.

fields.why_it_matters: Wander Nagaland sits 300m from the centre of Pfutsero, the highest-altitude town in Nagaland (2133m).
fields.insider_tip: The pre-arranged dinner thali is ₹250 per head.

fields.why_it_matters: Pfutseros main bazaar has half a dozen unnamed Chakhesang eateries that feed the towns ~17k residents.
fields.insider_tip: Open 8am–6pm; everything shuts down before 7pm.

fields.why_it_matters: Glory Peak (Pfutseros sunrise viewpoint over the Chakhesang highlands) has two or three permanent tea-shacks that open at 4:30am for the daily sunrise crowd.
fields.insider_tip: Sunrise hits the eastern ridges between 5:15am and 5:45am.

fields.why_it_matters: Cafe 4Zero is the only named cafe consistently flagged in coverage of Pfutsero town — the rest of the dining scene is what a 2018 traveller's account calls 'rice hotels' (basic local dhabas serving rice with fish/pork/mutton or dal-rice-vegetables). Pfutsero sits at ~2,133m, in Phek district, ~60km from Kohima; commercial dining is genuinely thin, and 4Zero is the most-recommended sit-down option for visitors during the day.
fields.insider_tip: Hours and menu vary day-to-day — call ahead via your homestay or Pfutsero tourism contact. For full meals, plan around lunch; evenings in Pfutsero shut down early. The town is high and cold most of the year — go for hot tea and smoked pork rather than the cold/cafe-style menu.

fields.why_it_matters: The community-owned Mini Tourist Lodge canteen is the only printed-menu eatery in Pfutsero town outside Cafe 4Zero — meals at ~₹120 breakfast / ₹200 lunch-dinner per traveller accounts. Pfutsero sits at 2,133m (highest inhabited town in Nagaland, pop 10,371 per 2011 census) and winter nights drop below 0°C — the kitchen pivots to hot smoked-pork thalis Nov-Feb when the cold-storage stalls outside shut early. Cherry-blossom season (Nov-Dec) drives the most footfall outside the Cosmos Zenith Festival weekend (Nov 8 in 2024).
fields.insider_tip: Book your room and your meals at the same time — the canteen runs to lodge numbers and won't reliably feed walk-ins. The Chakhesang smoked-pork preparation uses bamboo-shoot ferment (different from the Sema axone you'll find in Kohima) — ask for it with chokri-style chilli paste. Avoid post-7 PM dinner; the kitchen winds down for the cold.

fields.why_special: Modern boutique hotel — easily the best stay in Kohima. Clean rooms with Naga-inspired decor, a restaurant serving authentic Naga cuisine (smoked pork, axone chutney, raja mircha), and a rooftop bar. Walking distance to the WWII cemetery and local market.

Mid-range hotel with character — Naga tribal art on the walls, warm staff, and a restaurant that takes Naga food seriously. The smoked pork with bamboo shoot here rivals any home kitchen. Good base for Hornbill Festival visits (book 3 months ahead in December).

Small boutique hotel above a popular café. Just 8 rooms, each tastefully done with local textiles. The café downstairs is Kohima's social hub — great coffee, Naga snacks, and the best carrot cake in the Northeast. Book the top-floor room for church-and-mountain views.

Family-run cottages in the land of the Konyak Nagas. Simple but clean rooms and the host family shares stories of Konyak headhunting traditions (now peaceful, of course). They arrange visits to Longwa village where the chief's house straddles the India-Myanmar border.

Government guesthouse perched on a hilltop with views over Mon district. Basic but spacious rooms. The caretaker is a local Konyak who can arrange village visits and introductions to tattooed headhunters (the last generation). Book through Nagaland Tourism.

fields.why_nakshiq: On D.C. Hill, the highest point of Mokokchung — modern 3-star with a Naga-cuisine restaurant, licensed bar and 360° valley views; the canonical 'comfortable' stay for visiting Ao-Naga heartland. Address: D.C. Hill, Sangtemla Ward, Mokokchung 798601, Nagaland. Phone: 0369-2229743 / 9615166202.

Family-run guesthouse + homestay in Alongmen Ward, 3 minutes from the town square and bus stand — basic rooms, Ao hospitality, terrace 360° view; listed on the Naga Homestay collective and the cheapest decent option in town. Address: S.E. Colony Road, Alongmen Ward, Mokokchung 798601, Nagaland. Phone: +91 70855 78530.

Hilltop hotel above R. Kathing Park, 0.5 km from the centre — 10 spacious rooms, multi-cuisine restaurant, walking distance to the Town Hall and the Ao Senden building. The mid-range default since 1988. Address: R. Kathing Park, Mokokchung Compound, Mokokchung 798601, Nagaland. Phone: 0369-2226373 / 9436006169.

Community-managed homestays run by Angami families in Asia's first Green Village. Basic wood-and-stone village homes with traditional meals. The stay IS the experience — you see how the community's green-village model works day-to-day.
fields.signature_experience: Morning walk through Khonoma's stone-paved paths to the legacy terraced-rice fields (750 years old), with an Angami host explaining the village's hunting ban and forest-restoration story.

fields.why_nakshiq: We recommend it as Kohima's most established upscale property, with views over the city and reliable service for travellers seeking comfort in the northeast.
fields.signature_experience: Morning at Kohima War Cemetery (WWII-era Battle of Kohima site, 5-min drive) for the Commonwealth-graves walk, then drive to Khonoma (20 km) for the Angami-village visit.

fields.why_nakshiq: We recommend it for travellers seeking well-maintained rooms, on-site dining, and proximity to Kohima attractions at a mid-tier price point.
We recommend it for its central position near the main bazaar and walking distance to Kohima High School and local markets.
We recommend it as Mon's most polished stay, with en-suite rooms, restaurant service, and the reliability travellers expect when splurging in a remote Naga town.
We recommend this family-run guesthouse for clean rooms, local hospitality, and proximity to Mon's market—solid comfort without resort markup.
We recommend it for its position on Mon's main commercial street, steps from the market, Naga tribal museum, and local eateries.
We recommend this as Pfutsero's most established upscale property, offering heated rooms and valley views that justify the splurge for cold-season comfort at 2,100m elevation.
We recommend it because it sits 50m from the main bazaar and the viewpoint trail head, making morning walks to the valley rim feasible without a vehicle.
We recommend this if you want to sleep at Pfutsero's highest accessible point (2,140m) under stars with a wood stove inside thick canvas, watching sunrise over Assam plains before breakfast.
We recommend this because Kohima is the mandatory transit hub (20 km from Dzukou trailhead); Japfu is well-located in town center and runs reliable valley shuttle bookings.

The ONLY in-valley shelter — Forest Dept-run trekkers' dormitory at the trek-end (the structure beyond which the valley floor opens up). 30-bunk shared dorm, kitchen with caretaker who cooks pre-ordered Naga meals (book in Viswema/Jakhama before ascent), no power, basic. The closest you can sleep to Dzukou itself. First-come-first-served; carry sleeping bag.
fields.signature_experience: Pre-dawn walk from the hut onto the valley floor for the rolling-mist photographs that define Dzukou — peak season Jun-Sep (lily bloom), late-Oct-Nov (golden grass), Dec-Feb (frost).

fields.why_nakshiq: Rovi and Akienieo's family homestay in Kigwema village (at the Dzukou trailhead) — the canonical Dzukou trek base. Tripoto-canonical, run by Angami sisters who also operate trek logistics (porters, packed lunches, valley-end pickup). Home-cooked Angami meals (smoked pork with akhuni-fermented soybean, axone curry, bamboo-shoot pickle). 20km from Kohima, 5min from the Viswema trailhead.

Khonoma is Asia's first Green Village (Angami council banned hunting + logging, 2005) — a 700-year-old fortified Angami settlement 20km from Kohima. Cherry Blossom Cottages are stone-and-timber traditional homes converted into homestays, run by the village green-conservation council. Pair Dzukou with a Khonoma night — the cultural xfactor most trekkers skip. Angami Naga territory (NOT Zeme — that's Peren/Tamenglong).
fields.signature_experience: Walk the Khonoma terrace-rice fields with a council guide — 80-step morung-traditional architecture, the only village in India where the council formally manages biodiversity (Khonoma Tragopan Sanctuary).

fields.why_nakshiq: We recommend staying with local families here because you'll eat traditional Angami Naga meals, learn weaving, and spend a third of what resorts charge while funding village livelihoods directly.

6-room boutique inn inside Khonoma village — closest to the Sopfunuo (warrior's wife) memorial gate and the stone-paved path to the 750-year-old terraces. Cozy hill-view rooms; bird and butterfly walks arranged by the family. Address: Khonoma Village, Kohima District 797001, Nagaland.

Sangtemla Ward government circuit house — book through the DC office; basic but the only government-grade option, and the closest you get to a 'heritage administrative' stay in town. Address: Sangtemla Ward, Mokokchung 798601, Nagaland. Phone: 0369-22262618 / 7005177857.
We recommend it for direct access to Naga family life, home-cooked traditional meals, and hands-on learning of local weaving and craft traditions.

3-room family homestay run by Vikepeno and Apeno Pier — classic room ₹2,000, family room ₹2,600 (incl. breakfast); balcony view over Khonoma's terraced rice fields. Apeno's cooking and history stories are the draw. Address: Khonoma Village, Kohima District 797001, Nagaland (19 km from Kohima).

32-house Angami hamlet 8 km beyond Khonoma run as a TATA Trust eco-tourism cluster — basic homestays, trout streams, Blyth's tragopan birding; the 'further-in' stay for travellers who already did Khonoma village. Address: Dzuleke village, Kohima District, Nagaland (8 km west of Khonoma).
